title: Pressure. Pack. Do not peek.
body:
### Situation
Blood is leaving the person faster than you like. You can see it or the clothes are soaking.

### Do
1. Expose the site. Gloves. Find the hole, not just the soaked pant.
2. Direct pressure with cloth. Both hands. Hard. On the wound, not next to it.
3. If it soaks, do not take the first cloth off. Add more. Pack a deep hole with gauze or clean cloth and press.
4. If a limb is pumping and pressure fails, a tourniquet high and tight on that limb. Note the time.
5. Lie them down. Keep them warm. The next failure is cold and faint.
6. Do not keep peeking. Hold. Ten minutes is longer than you think.
7. Get to care. Write what you did and when.

### Cautions
- A trickle after a punchy fall can still be a lot of blood inside a boot.
- Improvised wraps that only circle the limb without pressure on the hole are decorations.
- Head and torso holes do not get a limb tourniquet. Pressure and pack, then move toward care.
summary: Expose, press hard, pack deep holes, tourniquet a pumping limb, keep them warm, get to care.

title: They twisted it. Decide if it walks.
body:
### Situation
A foot or knee went sideways. It swells. They want to try the trail. You need a walk-or-stay call.

### Do
1. Sit them. Pack off. Look at the joint. Compare to the other side.
2. If bone is poking, the joint is the wrong shape, or they felt a pop and cannot take any weight, treat as a fracture card.
3. Otherwise: rest, cold stream or snow in a cloth if it is close, compression wrap, elevate when stopped.
4. Tape or wrap in the boot they will walk in, not in a way that cuts the toes off.
5. Test: short level steps. If they can take weight with a pole and the trail is easy, go slow.
6. If they cannot take weight, or the trail is scree at dusk, this is a stay-and-signal or a carry you probably do not have.
7. Recheck swelling and color of toes. Loosen wrap if they go numb or blue.

### Cautions
- “Walk it off” on a 14er descent in the dark is how a sprain becomes a night out plus a fall.
- Numbness, cold white toes, or a wrap that is a tourniquet by accident: loosen.
- **Rockies**: talus hides holes. After a twist, shorten the day. The next hole is waiting.
summary: Compare joints, wrap and test on level ground. No weight plus hard trail means stay and signal.

title: Treat as if the bone is broken.
body:
### Situation
Wrong shape, bone out, they heard a crack, or they will not load the limb. You do not need an X-ray to stop using it.

### Do
1. Scene safe. Bleeding first if there is a hole.
2. Do not test it by twisting. Leave it in the position that they can stand if it is already there and circulation looks OK.
3. Pad. Splint the joints above and below with a pad, stay, or the other leg for a femur if that is all you have.
4. Check fingers or toes before and after: color, warmth, they can wiggle. If you lose that, loosen once.
5. Pain plus cold: warmth, food, water, and a pad under them while you wait.
6. This is not a walk-it-off. Signal and wait, or a planned carry toward care if you truly have the people and the trail.
7. Write time, what you saw, and what you splinted.

### Cautions
- Pulling a bone end back under the skin because it looks ugly can worsen bleeding. Get to care.
- A “maybe just a sprain” that cannot take weight on a remote slope is treated as a fracture for the night.
- Do not feed a person who may need a procedure soon if help is minutes away. If help is hours, small sips and warmth win.
summary: Do not test a wrong-shaped limb. Pad, splint above and below, check toes, stay and signal.

title: Cool the burn. Then cover it.
body:
### Situation
Stove flare, steam, hot pot, or a brush with the ring. Skin is angry or gone.

### Do
1. Stop the burning. Get them off the heat. Smother flame. Cool clothing if it is still hot and not melted into skin.
2. Cool with clean water 10–20 minutes. Not ice packed on the wound.
3. Remove tight things: rings, watches, hot belts, before swell.
4. Cover loosely with clean cloth. Do not pop every blister for fun.
5. Keep them warm. Burned people drop heat.
6. If the area is large, on the face, hands, genitals, or all the way around a limb, this is a get-to-care problem now.
7. Hydrate if they can drink and care is hours away.

### Cautions
- Butter, toothpaste, and mud are not dressings.
- Melted fabric stuck to skin stays. Cut around it.
- Do not use the last drinking water to flood a tiny finger burn if the group is already dry. A creek and then treat the remaining water.
summary: Stop the heat, cool with water, remove rings, loose clean cover, keep them warm, get to care if large.

title: Stop the hot spot while it is a hot spot.
body:
### Situation
A hot spot on a foot, heel, or pack strap. Tomorrow’s blister is still preventable.

### Do
1. Stop at the first complaint. Pack off. Sock off. Look.
2. Red hot skin: dry, then tape or a thin pad so the rub dies.
3. Closed blister that you can still walk on: pad around it, not a tight doughnut that becomes a pressure ring.
4. If it has torn and must be walked on: clean as you can, leave the roof if it is still a roof, dress, tape, dry sock.
5. Change to a dry sock. Grit in the sock is sandpaper.
6. Relace. Heel lock. Many blisters are a lacing problem, not a mystery.
7. Recheck at the next sit. Do not wait until blood is in the sock.

### Cautions
- Opening every blister in a dirty creek is a way to make a wound card.
- Duct tape on a wet hot spot can rip skin when you peel it. Use it over a film or paper if that is all you have.
- **Rockies**: long descents off 14ers grind heels. Tape before the downhill, not at the lake of regret.
summary: Stop at the hot spot, dry, tape, relace, dry sock. Dress a torn blister; do not excavate it in a creek.

title: They are cold in the middle, not just the hands.
body:
### Situation
Uncontrolled shivering, clumsy hands, mumbling, or “I’m fine” while they fumble a zipper. Wet plus wind is the usual recipe.

### Do
1. Stop heat loss: out of wind, off the ground, wet layer off the torso, dry or wrung layer on, wind shell on.
2. Insulate. Pad underneath. Hat. Dry socks. Shared quilt or bag if you have one.
3. Feed and water if they can swallow safely. Warm drink if you can make it without losing the shelter.
4. Buddy them. Do not send a clumsy person to “go get wood” alone.
5. If shivering stops and they are confused or slipping, this is a stay-and-signal emergency. Handle them gently.
6. Rewarm the trunk, not a fire roast of the hands that dumps cold blood.
7. After they improve, do not rush back into the same wet wind. Change the plan.

### Cautions
- Rubbing stone-cold arms, alcohol, and a forced march “to warm up” make this worse.
- A person who was shivering and then goes quiet is not “tough now.”
- **Rockies**: 50 F (10 C) rain on a June 13er is enough. Summer calendar does not block this card.
summary: Stop wind and wet, pad off the ground, fuel if they can swallow, trunk rewarm. Quiet after shivering is worse.

title: Pale, numb, frozen parts.
body:
### Situation
Fingers, toes, ears, or nose that are white or waxy, numb, or wooden. The rest of the person may still be talking.

### Do
1. Get out of the wind. Skin to warm skin for ears and nose if you can. Mitten the hands.
2. Do not rub snow on it. Do not beat it against a boot.
3. If you can reach a place the part will stay thawed, rewarm in warm water that is not scalding, 99–104 F (37–40 C) if you can measure. If you cannot measure, body-warm, not fire-hot.
4. If you must walk on a frozen foot to get to care, it may be better to walk frozen than to thaw and refreeze. That is a hard call. Favor getting to care without a second freeze.
5. Pad and splint a thawed part. It will hurt. Do not use it as a clamp.
6. Warm the whole person. Frostbite rides with hypothermia.
7. Get to care for white, wooden, or blistering parts.

### Cautions
- Fire and stove rewarm burns the numb skin you cannot feel.
- Refreeze after a field thaw is worse than a controlled walk on a still-frozen foot toward a real roof.
- **Rockies**: metal camera and axe heads, plus wind on a January Front Range ridge, will do this in minutes. Cover skin on the approach, not after it goes quiet.
summary: Wind off, no rubbing, rewarm only if it will not refreeze. Walk a frozen foot to care rather than thaw twice.

title: Too hot. Shade and sip.
body:
### Situation
Dizzy, nauseated, cramped, pounding head, or a person who is hot and not making sense on a climb.

### Do
1. Shade. Off black rock. Pack off. Fan them.
2. Loosen clothes. Cool neck, armpits, groin with water you can spare.
3. Sip water. Salt snack if they can keep it down.
4. If they are confused, collapsing, or the skin is hot and they are not sweating, cool hard and get to care. This is not a rest-and-go.
5. Legs up if they are faint and the scene is safe.
6. Descend when they can walk. Cooler air is treatment.
7. Hold the group. One more “short push” is how you carry someone.

### Cautions
- A person who stops sweating and stops making sense is not “getting used to it.”
- Piling on extra clothes because they have goosebumps while still in the sun is the wrong reflex if they are overheated.
- **Rockies**: foothill west faces in June plus Denver people who drove up at noon. There is almost no shade on the plains edge. Start earlier.
summary: Shade, cool, sip, descend. Hot, confused, and not sweating means cool hard and get to care.

title: The elevation is part of the picture.
body:
### Situation
Headache, nausea, odd fatigue, or clumsy thinking after a gain in elevation. You cannot name the diagnosis on the ridge. You can descend.

### Do
1. Stop the gain. Sit. Water. A snack. Sun off the head.
2. If the person is worse at rest, ataxic, confused, or gasping at rest, descend now. Do not wait for dawn on the summit.
3. Descent is the treatment you have. 1,000–2,000 ft (300–600 m) can change the picture.
4. Keep them warm and walking in control. No solo “I’ll catch up.”
5. Do not send them higher because the parking lot is on the other side of the peak unless that is truly shorter and downhill both ways — it almost never is.
6. Headache that improves with water and rest may just be that. Recheck before you climb again.
7. Get to care if descent does not improve them or they cannot walk a straight line.

### Cautions
- You do not get to call this “just dehydration” if they cannot tandem-walk and the lips are the wrong color.
- Sleeping higher after a bad day is a gamble. Down is the default.
- **Rockies**: Denver is already 5,280 ft (1609 m). Going to 14,000 ft (4267 m) in one morning is a common Front Range pattern. It is also a common fail.
summary: Stop climbing, water and rest, descend if they worsen at rest or cannot walk straight.

title: Clean what you can. Cover the rest.
body:
### Situation
A cut or scrape that is not pumping but is dirty. The trail is not a clinic. You can still make it worse.

### Do
1. Stop bleeding with pressure.
2. Irrigate with the cleanest water you have. Volume beats fancy. A stream from a bottle.
3. Pick out the obvious grit you can see. Do not excavate tunnels with a dirty knife.
4. Cover with a clean dressing. Change when soaked or filthy.
5. Watch for spreading red, fever, red streaks, or a wound that smells wrong the next day. That is a get-to-care flag.
6. Hands off. Do not keep poking it to show the group.
7. If it is deep, over a joint, from a bite, or you cannot stop the dirt, get to care.

### Cautions
- Super glue and duct tape on a dirty puncture trap the dirt.
- A puncture from a tool or a bite looks small and then goes deep. Take those to care.
- Do not use untreated ditch water as the irrigant if you have a treated bottle. Save a cup of treated for this.
summary: Pressure, irrigate with clean water, cover, watch for spreading red or fever, get to care if deep.

title: Pull the tick. Watch the skin.
body:
### Situation
A tick is in the skin, or you found one crawling. Spring foothills and brushy drainages are the usual story.

### Do
1. Tweezers close to the skin. Steady pull. Do not twist it into a trophy.
2. Do not burn it, grease it, or squeeze the body so it empties into the person.
3. Wash the site with soap or the cleanest water you have. Watch it.
4. Save the tick in a bag if you can. It helps later care. Do not play with it.
5. Note the date. A spreading bullseye or fever days later is a get-to-care problem. You do not name the disease on the trail.
6. Full skin check at night: belt line, behind knees, scalp, armpits, socks.
7. Pants into socks in brush. That is the field prevention that works.

### Cautions
- A rash or fever after a bite is not something to “wait and see” through a long trip. Get to care.
- Do not crush ticks with fingernails over the wound.
- **Rockies**: Front Range foothills in spring are tick country. High alpine is not a free pass on the hike out through oak brush.
summary: Tweezers at the skin, steady pull, wash, date it. Spreading rash or fever means get to care.

title: Bite. Keep still. Get to care.
body:
### Situation
A strike on a foot or hand, with or without a rattle you heard. You will not identify venom by folklore.

### Do
1. Move away from the snake. Do not hunt it.
2. Sit the person. Keep the bitten limb still and roughly at heart level if you can.
3. Remove rings and tight watches before swell.
4. Time it. Watch swelling and how they feel.
5. Walk them to care if that is faster than waiting in a place no one will find. Carry if you have the people. Running is not the plan.
6. Phone or messenger as soon as you have signal. This is a get-to-care problem.
7. Note color and pattern only if it costs you nothing. A photo from far away beats a second bite.

### Cautions
- No cutting, no sucking, no ice pack as treatment, no tourniquet as a default.
- A dry bite can still swell. Treat the person, not the story.
- **Rockies**: prairie rattlesnakes live on the Front Range foothills and hogback, not on the 14er talus. Watch hands on sunny rocks below about 8,000 ft (2440 m).
summary: Away from the snake, still limb, rings off, walk or carry to care. No cut, suck, or ice as treatment.
